what_its_for: Capecitabine is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, including breast cancer and colorectal cancer (cancer of the colon or rectum). It works by interfering with the growth of cancer cells and slowing or stopping their spread in the body.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablets whole with a full glass of water. Take capecitabine within 30 minutes after finishing a meal (breakfast and dinner). Do not crush, cut, or chew the tablets. Always take it exactly as your doctor tells you. If you have trouble swallowing the tablets, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before changing how you take them.
dosing: Capecitabine is usually taken twice a day — once in the morning and once in the evening, about 12 hours apart. It is typically taken for 14 days in a row, followed by a 7-day break (no medicine). This 21-day period is called one cycle. Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your body size and health. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it completely — do not try to make it up. Just take your next scheduled dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store capecitabine tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Store in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the safest way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking blood thinners like warfarin (Coumadin) without close monitoring, as capecitabine can increase the risk of serious bleeding. Avoid taking antacids containing aluminum or magnesium within 2 hours of your dose unless your doctor approves. Avoid getting vaccines (especially live vaccines) without checking with your doctor first. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as your skin may be more sensitive. Avoid alcohol unless your doctor says it is okay. Avoid handling broken or crushed tablets — if a tablet breaks, avoid skin contact and wash hands immediately.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: severe diarrhea (4 or more loose stools per day above your normal), nausea or vomiting that prevents you from eating or drinking, hand-foot syndrome (redness, swelling, blistering, peeling, or severe pain on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet), mouth sores that make it hard to eat or drink, fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (this could be a sign of infection), unusual bleeding or bruising, chest pain or shortness of breath, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Capecitabine starts working right away at the cellular level, but you may not notice visible changes for several weeks or months. Your doctor will monitor your progress through regular blood tests, imaging scans, and check-ups. It is very important to complete all planned cycles of treatment even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Elderly patients (65 and older): Side effects such as diarrhea and hand-foot syndrome may be more severe. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Kidney problems: If your kidneys do not work well, your doctor will adjust your dose. Capecitabine should NOT be used if you have severe kidney disease. Liver problems: Use with caution; your doctor will monitor your liver closely. Pregnancy: Do NOT take capecitabine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking capecitabine or for 2 weeks after your last dose. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
